newsitem.title: COMOROS: 56 missing, feared dead, from Ethiopian hijack.
newsitem.headline: 56 missing, feared dead, from Ethiopian hijack.

text.p: Fifty-six people were missing and feared dead on Sunday as rescuers searched the underwater wreckage of a hijacked Ethiopian Airlines plane that crashed off the Comoros Islands after running out of fuel.
Witnesses said divers had worked through the night after the plane broke into three pieces just off the shoreline of the main island of the Indian Ocean archipelago on Saturday.
At least 67 people died.
Fifty-two on board the Boeing 767 flight ET 961 survived, according to Ethiopian Airlines' main office in Addis Ababa.
Some managed to swim to shore only 500 metres (yards) away, while others bobbed helplessly in azure waters as sunbathing tourists rushed off the palm-fringed Le Galawa beach to help.
Rescuers said on Sunday they needed at least 36 hours and special equipment to recover between 50 to 70 bodies trapped in the submerged wreckage.

Captain Bruno Beausse, commanding a team of 15 French rescue divers who flew in from the Indian Ocean island of Reunion, said he would need heavy cutting equipment, underwater lighting and protective gear for his men before work could continue.
Earlier the pilot of the plane said the three men who tried to divert the craft to Australia wanted to "make history".

Their motives were unknown but the plan went horribly wrong as the plane, bound from Addis Ababa to Abidjan and due to have stopped in Nairobi, ran out of fuel some 25 km (16 miles) short of the airport at Moroni, capital of the four-island chain.
Two of the hijackers were among the survivors.
"We have now established the identity of the two hijackers who are in detention in the Comoros. They are Ethiopian," Ethiopian Airlines General Manager Ahmed Kello told Reuters.
The fate and nationality of the third were unknown.
One hijacker was reported to have been armed with an axe. Another wielded a fire extinguisher. The third had what he said was a bomb in one hand and a whisky bottle in the other.
Medical sources said three more bodies had washed ashore and divers pulled others from the fuselage on Sunday morning.
Among the survivors was the Ethiopian pilot, Leul Abate, 42, who suffered head injuries. He told Reuters from his bed at the El Maarouf hospital that there were three hijackers on board.
The U.S. consul general in Bombay, Franklin Huddle, and his wife also survived.

"I thought I was dead when we hit the water," Huddle said, describing how he and his wife managed to swim free of the wreckage and headed for the nearest windsurfer, which they clung to until they were taken to shore.

"They were not high-tech hijackers -- threatening types in the Middle East style. They let you get up to pee. But they were terrorists and they did not let the pilot communicate with us," Huddle said.
An Israeli passenger thrown into the sea during the crash said he managed to rescue a woman and her baby.

"We simply went into an emergency landing in the sea and I felt a powerful shaking. I was thrown from the seat, and water penetrated the plane, and somehow I managed to get out. I don't know how," Lior Fox, 23, told Israel Radio.

"I saw a woman with a baby who was caught, and I swam towards her and freed them from the wreckage and inflated the life preserver for her, and for the baby I inflated the life preserver, and we got up together on a boat," Fox said.
Top African television cameraman Mohamed Amin was believed to be among the passengers but his fate was still uncertain.
Amin, 53, of Reuters Television, won acclaim for bringing Ethiopia's disastrous 1984 famine to the eyes of the world.
The airline said it would delay until late on Sunday afternoon issuing a full list of passengers because of difficulties in compiling it.
Leul said one hijacker was wielding a small axe, apparently one kept in the plane for use in emergencies. A second carried a small fire extinguisher from the plane, wielding it as a weapon.
The third said he had a bomb in one hand, although Leul could not identify the object as such. In his other hand was a bottle of whisky.
They wanted to go to Australia but made no other demands, Leul said, adding: "The hijackers wanted to make history."
He said the three forced their way into the cockpit and beat up the co-pilot, Yonas Mekuria, 35, before throwing him out into the main body of the aircraft.
At one point a hijacker tried to fly the plane himself and wrenched the headset from Leul.
As a result, the pilot said he was unable to speak to air control personnel as the plane neared the Comoros. Earlier reports said there was brief contact with the control tower, but it was then cut.
